claim: OCT4 and SOX2 are pioneer transcription factors.
source: The OCT4 (encoded by Pou5f1) and SOX2 pioneer TFs (Soufi et al., 2015) are absolutely required for the self-renewal of embryonic stem (ES) cells (Masui et al., 2007; Niwa et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript cites Soufi et al., 2015 as support for OCT4 and SOX2 being pioneer TFs.

claim: OCT4 and SOX2 are absolutely required for the self-renewal of embryonic stem (ES) cells.
source: The OCT4 (encoded by Pou5f1) and SOX2 pioneer TFs (Soufi et al., 2015) are absolutely required for the self-renewal of embryonic stem (ES) cells (Masui et al., 2007; Niwa et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript cites Masui et al., 2007 and Niwa et al., 2000 as support for this requirement.

claim: OCT4 and SOX2 can form a heterodimer that binds to a composite motif at thousands of sites in the genome.
source: OCT4 and SOX2 can form a heterodimer that binds to a composite motif at thousands of sites in the genome (Boyer et al., 2005; Nishimoto et al., 1999; Yuan et al., 1995).
evidence: The manuscript cites Boyer et al., 2005; Nishimoto et al., 1999; Yuan et al., 1995 as support for heterodimer formation and binding.

claim: Depletion of OCT4 for 24 hr in ES cells leads to loss of accessibility and co-factor occupancy at a large fraction of its bound enhancers involved in pluripotency maintenance.
source: A recent study has shown that depletion of OCT4 for 24 hr in ES cells leads to loss of accessibility and co-factor occupancy at a large fraction of its bound enhancers involved in pluripotency maintenance (King and Klose, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites King and Klose, 2017 as support for this finding.

claim: Chromatin accessibility of gene regulatory elements is markedly decreased during S phase and mitosis.
source: This is not a trivial task since chromatin accessibility of gene regulatory elements is markedly decreased during S phase and mitosis (Festuccia et al., 2019; Hsiung et al., 2015; Oomen et al., 2019; Stewart-Morgan et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites Festuccia et al., 2019; Hsiung et al., 2015; Oomen et al., 2019; Stewart-Morgan et al., 2019 as support for this observation.

claim: OCT4 expression levels in G1 phase affect the propensity of ES cells to differentiate towards neuroectoderm and mesendoderm.
source: OCT4 expression levels in G1 phase affect the propensity of ES cells to differentiate towards neuroectoderm and mesendoderm (Strebinger et al., 2019)
evidence: The manuscript cites Strebinger et al., 2019 as support for this finding.

claim: Depletion of OCT4 at the M-G1 transition impairs pluripotency maintenance of ES cells and leads to a lower reprogramming efficiency upon overexpression in mouse embryonic fibroblasts.
source: depletion of OCT4 at the M-G1 transition impairs pluripotency maintenance of ES cells and leads to a lower reprogramming efficiency upon overexpression in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites Liu et al., 2017 as support for this finding.

claim: Depletion of SOX2 at the M-G1 transition impairs both pluripotency maintenance and SOX2-induced neuroectodermal differentiation of ES cells upon release of pluripotency signals.
source: Depletion of SOX2 at the M-G1 transition impairs both pluripotency maintenance and SOX2-induced neuroectodermal differentiation of ES cells upon release of pluripotency signals (Deluz et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites Deluz et al., 2016 as support for this finding.

claim: OCT4 and SOX2 regulate chromatin accessibility at mostly distinct loci.
source: OCT4 and SOX2 regulate chromatin accessibility at mostly distinct loci
evidence: This is a section heading that summarizes findings presented in the Results section, supported by experimental ATAC-seq data.

claim: OCT4 is fully depleted after 24 hr of doxycycline treatment in ZHBTc4 cells.
source: While OCT4 is fully depleted after 24 hr of doxycycline (dox) (Niwa et al., 2000)
evidence: The manuscript cites Niwa et al., 2000 as support for this observation.

claim: SOX2 is not fully depleted after 24 hr of doxycycline treatment, likely due to its longer half-life.
source: SOX2 is not, likely due to its longer half-life (Masui et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites Masui et al., 2007 and provides inference about the reason for incomplete depletion.

claim: Residual SOX2 expression persisted after 26 hr but not 40 hr of dox treatment.
source: We determined SOX2 levels by immunofluorescence staining after 26 and 40 hr of dox treatment and found that residual SOX2 expression persisted after 26 hr but not 40 hr of dox treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: SOX2 depletion for 26 or 40 hr had only a minor impact on OCT4 levels.
source: Importantly, despite its known role in regulating expression of OCT4 (Dunn et al., 2014; Strebinger et al., 2019), SOX2 depletion for 26 or 40 hr had only a minor impact on OCT4 levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The manuscript presents data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B and cites Dunn et al., 2014; Strebinger et al., 2019 for the known role of SOX2 in regulating OCT4.

claim: 24 hr of dox treatment in ZHBTc4 cells led to the complete depletion of OCT4 and only mildly affected SOX2 levels.
source: In ZHBTc4 cells, as expected, 24 hr of dox treatment led to the complete depletion of OCT4 and only mildly affected SOX2 levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The manuscript presents data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: Loss of OCT4 led to decreased accessibility at 20,587 loci, most of which are distal regulatory elements.
source: In line with previous reports, loss of OCT4 led to decreased accessibility at 20'587 loci, most of which are distal regulatory elements (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript presents data shown in Figure 1B and references previous reports.

claim: Loss of SOX2 led to decreased accessibility mainly at distal elements, but at fewer loci (7,874).
source: Loss of SOX2 also led to decreased accessibility mainly at distal elements, but at fewer loci (7'874).
evidence: The manuscript presents data from ATAC-seq experiments.

claim: Loss of OCT4 led to a gain in accessibility at 20,209 loci.
source: We also found that loss of OCT4 led to a gain in accessibility at 20'209 loci
evidence: The manuscript presents data from ATAC-seq experiments.

claim: Loss of SOX2 led to a gain in accessibility at 1,080 loci.
source: while 1'080 loci gained accessibility upon loss of SOX2 (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript presents data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Loci that lost accessibility were highly enriched for OCT4 and SOX2 ChIP-seq binding.
source: Loci that lost accessibility were highly enriched for OCT4 and SOX2 ChIP-seq binding while loci that gained accessibility were much less so (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: The manuscript presents ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: 8,869 loci were classified as OCT4-dependent (OD), defined by loss of accessibility upon depletion of OCT4 only.
source: We classified the remaining loci as OCT4-dependent (OD, 8'869 loci), SOX2-dependent (SD, 1'834 loci), and co-dependent (CD, 2'973 loci), as defined by loss of accessibility upon depletion of OCT4 only, SOX2 only, or either of them, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, Figure 1C–E).
evidence: The manuscript presents data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and Figure 1C–E.

claim: 1,834 loci were classified as SOX2-dependent (SD), defined by loss of accessibility upon depletion of SOX2 only.
source: We classified the remaining loci as OCT4-dependent (OD, 8'869 loci), SOX2-dependent (SD, 1'834 loci), and co-dependent (CD, 2'973 loci), as defined by loss of accessibility upon depletion of OCT4 only, SOX2 only, or either of them, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, Figure 1C–E).
evidence: The manuscript presents data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and Figure 1C–E.

claim: 2,973 loci were classified as co-dependent (CD), defined by loss of accessibility upon depletion of either OCT4 or SOX2.
source: We classified the remaining loci as OCT4-dependent (OD, 8'869 loci), SOX2-dependent (SD, 1'834 loci), and co-dependent (CD, 2'973 loci), as defined by loss of accessibility upon depletion of OCT4 only, SOX2 only, or either of them, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, Figure 1C–E).
evidence: The manuscript presents data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and Figure 1C–E.

claim: All three groups (OD, CD, SD) were enriched for chromatin marks of enhancers.
source: All three groups were enriched for chromatin marks of enhancers (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The manuscript presents ChromHMM data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: All groups (OD, CD, SD) displayed a reduction in H3K27ac upon OCT4 or SOX2 loss.
source: All groups displayed a reduction in H3K27ac, suggesting concordant maintenance of enhancer accessibility and activity by OCT4 and/or SOX2 at these loci (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: The manuscript presents H3K27ac ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1F–G.

claim: 89% of SD sites overlapped with an OCT4 peak.
source: 89% of SD sites overlapped with an OCT4 peak and 65% of OD sites overlapped with a SOX2 peak.
evidence: The manuscript presents analysis of ChIP-seq peak overlap.

claim: 65% of OD sites overlapped with a SOX2 peak.
source: 89% of SD sites overlapped with an OCT4 peak and 65% of OD sites overlapped with a SOX2 peak.
evidence: The manuscript presents analysis of ChIP-seq peak overlap.

claim: OCT4 regulates chromatin accessibility by recruitment of the BAF chromatin remodeling complex, including the BRG1 subunit.
source: OCT4 has been shown to regulate chromatin accessibility by recruitment of the BAF chromatin remodeling complex, including the BRG1 subunit (King and Klose, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites King and Klose, 2017 as support for this mechanism.

claim: SOX2 interacts with BRG1 in vivo.
source: As SOX2 also interacts with BRG1 in vivo (Xu et al., 2018)
evidence: The manuscript cites Xu et al., 2018 as support for this interaction.

claim: Loss of accessibility was accompanied by loss of BRG1 in all groups (OD, CD, SD).
source: We found that loss of accessibility was accompanied by loss of BRG1 in all groups (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: The manuscript presents BRG1 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2B–C.

claim: All groups (OD, CD, SD) were dependent on BRG1 to maintain their accessibility.
source: We also reanalyzed ATAC-seq data from cells in which BRG1 has been depleted (Ho et al., 2011; King and Klose, 2017) and found that all groups were dependent on BRG1 to maintain their accessibility (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reanalyzed published ATAC-seq data from Ho et al., 2011; King and Klose, 2017 and presents results in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: OCT4 and SOX2 can regulate chromatin accessibility independently of each other even at sites that are co-occupied and through the recruitment of BRG1.
source: This suggests that OCT4 and SOX2 can regulate chromatin accessibility independently of each other even at sites that are co-occupied and through the recruitment of BRG1.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing independent regulation despite co-occupancy.

claim: Both OD and CD loci were strongly enriched for the OCT4::SOX2 canonical motif and the OCT motif.
source: While both OD and CD loci were strongly enriched for the OCT4::SOX2 canonical motif and the OCT motif, SD loci were more enriched for the SOX motif (Figure 2D–F and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents motif analysis data shown in Figure 2D–F and Supplementary file 2.

claim: SD loci were more enriched for the SOX motif.
source: While both OD and CD loci were strongly enriched for the OCT4::SOX2 canonical motif and the OCT motif, SD loci were more enriched for the SOX motif (Figure 2D–F and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents motif analysis data shown in Figure 2D–F and Supplementary file 2.

claim: SD sites were enriched for the AP-2 motif.
source: SD sites were also enriched for the AP-2 motif (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript presents motif analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TFAP2C, a member of the AP-2 family, regulates differentiation into trophoblast stem (TS) cells together with SOX2.
source: TFAP2C, a member of the AP-2 family, is known to regulate differentiation into trophoblast stem (TS) cells together with SOX2 (Adachi et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites Adachi et al., 2013 as support for this regulatory relationship.

claim: SD sites are highly accessible and SOX2-bound in TS cells compared to OD and CD loci.
source: Interestingly, when reanalyzing data from TS cells (Adachi et al., 2013; Ishiuchi et al., 2019) we found SD sites to be highly accessible and SOX2-bound compared to OD and CD loci (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The manuscript reanalyzed published data from Adachi et al., 2013; Ishiuchi et al., 2019 and presents results in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: SD loci were enriched near genes that increased in nascent mRNA expression upon loss of OCT4.
source: Furthermore, SD loci were enriched near genes that increased in nascent mRNA expression upon loss of OCT4 (data from King and Klose, 2017) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: The manuscript reanalyzed data from King and Klose, 2017 and presents results in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: OD and CD loci were enriched near genes that decreased in nascent mRNA expression upon OCT4 depletion.
source: In contrast, OD and CD loci were enriched near genes that decreased in nascent mRNA expression upon OCT4 depletion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript presents data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Pluripotency-associated gene ontology sets tended to be most highly enriched in genes near OD loci.
source: We found that these GO sets tended to be most highly enriched in genes near OD loci, although all groups were enriched in at least one of the GO sets (Figure 2G–I).
evidence: The manuscript presents gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2G–I.

claim: The highest enrichment of pluripotency TFs (ESRRB, NANOG, KLF4, SALL4) was found in the CD group.
source: We also analyzed the binding profiles of other pluripotency TFs (ESRRB, NANOG, KLF4, SALL4) (data from Aksoy et al., 2014; Chronis et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2018; Xiong et al., 2016) and found the highest enrichment in the CD group, although all these TFs bound to some extent to all groups of loci (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The manuscript reanalyzed published ChIP-seq data from Aksoy et al., 2014; Chronis et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2018; Xiong et al., 2016 and presents results in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: All groups (OD, CD, SD) were enriched for the 'cell differentiation' GO term.
source: Notably, all groups were also enriched for the 'cell differentiation' GO term (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), in line with the role of OCT4 and SOX2 in ES cell differentiation.
evidence: The manuscript presents gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: SOX2 was shown to require PARP1 to bind to a subset of genomic regions in ES cells.
source: Since SOX2 was shown to require PARP1 to bind to a subset of genomic regions in ES cells (Liu and Kraus, 2017)
evidence: The manuscript cites Liu and Kraus, 2017 as support for this requirement.

claim: A reduction of SOX2 binding in PARP1 KO cells was found at all groups of loci (OD, CD, SD).
source: We thus reanalyzed data from wt and PARP1 knockout (KO) ES cells (Gao et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2004), and found a reduction of SOX2 binding in PARP1 KO cells at all groups of loci (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The manuscript reanalyzed published data from Gao et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2004 and presents results in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: PARP1 dependence cannot explain the differential regulation of chromatin accessibility between OD, CD, and SD loci.
source: Thus, PARP1 dependence cannot explain the differential regulation of chromatin accessibility between OD, CD, and SD loci.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that all groups show similar PARP1 dependence.

claim: OCT4 and SOX2 regulate partially independent sets of pluripotency and differentiation enhancers, with OCT4 having the largest influence on chromatin accessibility of pluripotency-associated regulatory elements.
source: Overall, these results indicate that OCT4 and SOX2 regulate partially independent sets of pluripotency and differentiation enhancers, with OCT4 having the largest influence on chromatin accessibility of pluripotency-associated regulatory elements.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from multiple experimental observations presented in the Results section.

claim: In vitro electrophoretic mobility shift assays and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy experiments have shown that OCT4 and SOX2 display enhanced binding to the OCT4::SOX2 motif when binding together.
source: In vitro electrophoretic mobility shift assays and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy experiments have shown that OCT4 and SOX2 display enhanced binding to the OCT4::SOX2 motif when binding together (Mistri et al., 2015; Mistri et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites Mistri et al., 2015; Mistri et al., 2018 as support for this observation.

claim: In vitro experiments reported OCT4-assisted binding on a purified nucleosomal template.
source: While in vitro experiments reported OCT4-assisted binding on a purified nucleosomal template (Li et al., 2019)
evidence: The manuscript cites Li et al., 2019 as support for this observation.

claim: Single-molecule imaging in live ES cells and ChIP-seq analysis of OCT4 in the presence or absence of SOX2 in fibroblasts have provided evidence that SOX2 assists OCT4 binding in vivo.
source: single-molecule imaging in live ES cells (Chen et al., 2014) and ChIP-seq analysis of OCT4 in the presence or absence of SOX2 in fibroblasts (Raccaud et al., 2019) have provided evidence that SOX2 assists OCT4 binding in vivo.
evidence: The manuscript cites Chen et al., 2014 and Raccaud et al., 2019 as support for this observation.

claim: Upon loss of OCT4, SOX2 binding loss is correlated to the loss in chromatin accessibility.
source: In line with this hypothesis, it was previously shown that upon loss of OCT4, SOX2 binding loss is correlated to the loss in chromatin accessibility (King and Klose, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites King and Klose, 2017 as support for this correlation.

claim: Changes in OCT4 binding were highly correlated to changes in chromatin accessibility upon SOX2 loss (Pearson's R = 0.77).
source: We found that changes in OCT4 binding were also highly correlated to changes in chromatin accessibility upon SOX2 loss (Pearson's R = 0.77) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript presents correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: OCT4 binding was only slightly decreased at OD sites in the absence of SOX2.
source: We found that OCT4 binding was only slightly decreased at OD sites in the absence of SOX2, while SOX2 binding at SD sites was mildly increased in the absence of OCT4 (Figure 2J–K).
evidence: The manuscript presents ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2J–K.

claim: SOX2 binding at SD sites was mildly increased in the absence of OCT4.
source: We found that OCT4 binding was only slightly decreased at OD sites in the absence of SOX2, while SOX2 binding at SD sites was mildly increased in the absence of OCT4 (Figure 2J–K).
evidence: The manuscript presents ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2J–K.

claim: Upon loss of its partner protein, OCT4 loses binding at 8,324 loci (of which 7,638 are called OCT4 peaks, representing 31% of OCT4 sites).
source: Upon loss of its partner protein, OCT4 loses binding at 8'324 loci (of which 7'638 are called OCT4 peaks, representing 31% of OCT4 sites)
evidence: The manuscript presents ChIP-seq analysis results.

claim: Upon loss of its partner protein, OCT4 gains binding at 739 loci (of which 212 are called OCT4 peaks, representing 1% of OCT4 sites).
source: and gains binding at 739 loci (of which 212 are called OCT4 peaks, representing 1% of OCT4 sites).
evidence: The manuscript presents ChIP-seq analysis results.

source: Conversely, SOX2 loses binding at 6'892 loci (of which 5'302 are called SOX2 peaks, representing 29% of SOX2 sites)
evidence: The manuscript presents ChIP-seq analysis results.

claim: Upon loss of OCT4, SOX2 gains binding at 4,136 loci (of which 983 are called SOX2 peaks, representing 5% of SOX2 sites).
source: and gains binding at 4'136 loci (of which 983 are called SOX2 peaks, representing 5% of SOX2 sites).
evidence: The manuscript presents ChIP-seq analysis results.

claim: The ability of OCT4 to occupy its specific binding sites is more impacted by the absence of SOX2 than vice-versa.
source: This indicates that the ability of OCT4 to occupy its specific binding sites is more impacted by the absence of SOX2 than vice-versa, and that SOX2 can get rerouted to new loci in the absence of OCT4.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ChIP-seq data showing differential impacts on binding.

claim: SOX2 can get rerouted to new loci in the absence of OCT4.
source: This indicates that the ability of OCT4 to occupy its specific binding sites is more impacted by the absence of SOX2 than vice-versa, and that SOX2 can get rerouted to new loci in the absence of OCT4.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ChIP-seq data showing SOX2 gaining binding at new sites.

claim: Loci gaining accessibility upon loss of OCT4 are enriched for differentiation terms.
source: We further noticed that loci gaining accessibility upon loss of OCT4, which are enriched for differentiation terms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G)
evidence: The manuscript presents gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Loci gaining accessibility upon loss of OCT4 also gained binding by SOX2.
source: We further noticed that loci gaining accessibility upon loss of OCT4, which are enriched for differentiation terms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), also gained binding by SOX2 (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2A columns 6–7 bottom half)
evidence: The manuscript presents data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Loci gaining accessibility upon loss of OCT4 were enriched for the SOX and AP-2 motifs.
source: and were enriched for the SOX and AP-2 motifs (Supplementary file 2).

source: and gained BRG1 occupancy concomitantly with OCT4 loss (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G), in line with SOX2 recruiting the BAF complex to promote chromatin opening.
evidence: The manuscript presents BRG1 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2G.

claim: OCT4 may sequester SOX2 to OCT4-SOX2 sites, and upon OCT4 loss SOX2 is free to bind and increase the accessibility of differentiation-associated regulatory elements.
source: This may suggest that OCT4 sequesters SOX2 to OCT4-SOX2 sites, and upon OCT4 loss SOX2 is free to bind and increase the accessibility of differentiation-associated regulatory elements.

source: Overall, these results indicate that cooperative binding of OCT4 and SOX2 in ES cells is mainly mediated indirectly through changes in chromatin accessibility.

claim: MAPK signaling promotes the exit from the naïve pluripotent state.

claim: Loci in clusters 1–3 were enriched near genes annotated for PI3K-Akt signaling, which is involved in the regulation of pluripotency.
source: Loci in clusters 1–3 were enriched near genes annotated for PI3K-Akt signaling, which is also involved in the regulation of pluripotency (Yu and Cui, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript presents gene ontology enrichment analysis and cites Yu and Cui, 2016.

claim: All three OCT4-dependent clusters contain regulatory elements involved in pluripotency maintenance.
source: This suggests that all three OCT4-dependent clusters contain regulatory elements involved in pluripotency maintenance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gene ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: Super-enhancers (SEs) and 'typical' enhancers (TEs) are enriched in all clusters compared to non-OCT4 bound accessible regions, with slightly more enrichment in clusters 1 and 3 for both SEs and TEs.
source: We found these to be enriched in all clusters compared to non-OCT4 bound accessible regions, with slightly more enrichment in clusters 1 and 3 for both SEs and TEs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The manuscript presents overlap analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: A large fraction of both SEs and TEs are affected across one cell cycle by the transient loss of OCT4 at the M-G1 transition.
source: This suggests that a large fraction of both SEs and TEs are affected across one cell cycle by the transient loss of OCT4 at the M-G1 transition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the overlap analysis.

claim: Pluripotency is maintained at lower than wildtype OCT4 expression levels.
source: As mentioned above, pluripotency was shown to be maintained at lower than wildtype OCT4 expression levels.
evidence: This refers to previously cited literature (Karwacki-Neisius et al., 2013; Radzisheuskaya et al., 2013).

claim: Only very minor differences in chromatin accessibility were found between cells expressing high versus low endogenous levels of OCT4 across all clusters.
source: We compared chromatin accessibility of the clusters for cells expressing high versus low endogenous levels of OCT4 and found only very minor differences in chromatin accessibility between these groups across all clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D), consistent with the ability of moderately low OCT4 levels to fully sustain pluripotency.
evidence: The manuscript presents ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D.

claim: A higher enrichment for the canonical OCT4::SOX2 motif was found at cluster 1 loci.
source: We found a higher enrichment for the canonical OCT4::SOX2 motif (Figure 3E) and a higher OCT4 occupancy (Figure 3F) at cluster 1 loci.
evidence: The manuscript presents motif analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A higher OCT4 occupancy was found at cluster 1 loci.
source: We found a higher enrichment for the canonical OCT4::SOX2 motif (Figure 3E) and a higher OCT4 occupancy (Figure 3F) at cluster 1 loci.
evidence: The manuscript presents ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Cluster 1 contained mostly OD and CD loci.
source: Consistently, cluster 1 contained mostly OD and CD loci identified above (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: The manuscript presents overlap analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3E.

claim: High OCT4 binding is a signature of the loci most sensitive to transient OCT4 loss.
source: As high OCT4 binding was a signature of the loci most sensitive to transient OCT4 loss
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the clustering and ChIP-seq analysis.

claim: The OCT4 ChIP-seq signal was correlated to loss of accessibility upon OCT4 depletion.
source: The OCT4 ChIP-seq signal was correlated to loss of accessibility upon OCT4 depletion (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A) as shown previously
evidence: The manuscript presents correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The OCT4 ChIP-seq signal was correlated to chromatin accessibility in untreated cells.
source: but also to chromatin accessibility in untreated cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B), indicating that strong OCT4 binding sites are both highly accessible and sensitive to OCT4 levels.
evidence: The manuscript presents correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Strong OCT4 binding sites are both highly accessible and sensitive to OCT4 levels.
source: but also to chromatin accessibility in untreated cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B), indicating that strong OCT4 binding sites are both highly accessible and sensitive to OCT4 levels.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation analysis.

claim: Several pluripotency-associated factors including DAX1, SOX2, NANOG, and SALL4 were enriched in clusters 1 and 3.
source: We identified several factors associated with pluripotency enriched in clusters 1 and 3, including DAX1, SOX2, NANOG, and SALL4.
evidence: The manuscript presents analysis of ChIP-seq data from cistromeDB.

claim: SALL4, NANOG, ESRRB, SOX2, and TBX3 were most enriched in cluster 1.
source: We confirmed that all of these factors tended to be enriched in clusters 1 and 3, and in particular SALL4, NANOG, ESRRB, SOX2, and TBX3, which were most enriched in cluster 1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4D) (data from Aksoy et al., 2014; Beck et al., 2014; Chronis et al., 2017; Deluz et al., 2016; Han et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2018; Stevens et al., 2017; Xiong et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript presents ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4D and cites multiple sources.

claim: A depletion of RAD21 (a Cohesin subunit) and CTCF was found in cluster 1.
source: We also found a depletion of RAD21 (a Cohesin subunit) and CTCF in cluster 1, in line with the differential enrichment of the CTCF motif.
evidence: The manuscript presents analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: Both RAD21 and CTCF are involved in the regulation of genome organization.
source: Indeed, both RAD21 and CTCF, which are involved in the regulation of genome organization (Phillips-Cremins et al., 2013), were poorly bound in cluster 1 compared to the other clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 4E) (data from Cattoglio et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites Phillips-Cremins et al., 2013 and presents ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4E from Cattoglio et al., 2019.

claim: Sites highly occupied by OCT4 and other pluripotency factors and lowly occupied by CTCF/Cohesin are particularly sensitive to OCT4 loss for the maintenance of their accessibility and H3K27 acetylation.
source: Taken together, these results reveal different classes of OCT4-bound loci that show different cell cycle accessibility dynamics upon OCT4 loss at the M-G1 transition, and that sites highly occupied by OCT4 and other pluripotency factors and lowly occupied by CTCF/Cohesin are particularly sensitive to OCT4 loss for the maintenance of their accessibility and H3K27 acetylation.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: Upon addition of indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), the AID-tagged OCT4 displayed an exponential degradation profile with a half-life of 0.32 hr.
source: Upon addition of indole-3-acetic acid (IAA, also known as Auxin), the AID-tagged OCT4 displayed an exponential degradation profile with a half-life of 0.32 hr (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript presents time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: After IAA washout, OCT4 recovered to approximately half of the concentration before IAA treatment within 4.5 hr.
source: After IAA washout, OCT4 recovered to approximately half of the concentration before IAA treatment within 4.5 hr (Figure 4C), in line with the OCT4 protein half-life of ~4 hr (Alber et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript presents time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 4C and cites Alber et al., 2018.

claim: The OCT4 protein half-life is ~4 hr.
source: After IAA washout, OCT4 recovered to approximately half of the concentration before IAA treatment within 4.5 hr (Figure 4C), in line with the OCT4 protein half-life of ~4 hr (Alber et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites Alber et al., 2018 as support for this half-life value.

claim: Auxin-mediated protein degradation is cell cycle-independent.
source: We observed highly similar changes in the mCherry signal across all cell cycle phases (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–E), consistent with previous reports on the cell cycle-independence of Auxin-mediated protein degradation (Holland et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–E and cites Holland et al., 2012.

claim: The relative magnitude of change in accessibility in the different clusters upon IAA treatment was consistent with the mitotic degradation experiment.
source: The relative magnitude of change in accessibility in the different clusters was consistent with our mitotic degradation experiment (Figure 4D).
evidence: The manuscript presents ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The average loss of accessibility was very similar at all cell cycle phases in clusters 1–3 upon IAA treatment.
source: Remarkably, the average loss of accessibility was very similar at all cell cycle phases in clusters 1–3 (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: The manuscript presents ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: Loci in clusters 1–3, and cluster 1 in particular, are sensitive to OCT4 throughout the cell cycle and not merely at the M-G1 transition.
source: This suggests that loci in clusters 1–3, and cluster 1 in particular, are sensitive to OCT4 throughout the cell cycle and not merely at the M-G1 transition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ATAC-seq data showing similar accessibility loss across cell cycle phases.

claim: Both cluster 1 and 2 recovered chromatin accessibility after IAA washout.
source: While both cluster 1 and 2 recovered chromatin accessibility, cluster 3 loci did not (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2C–E)
evidence: The manuscript presents ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2C–E.

claim: Cluster 3 loci did not recover chromatin accessibility after IAA washout.
source: While both cluster 1 and 2 recovered chromatin accessibility, cluster 3 loci did not (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2C–E), in line with their decrease of accessibility over the cell cycle upon OCT4 degradation at the M-G1 transition (see Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript presents ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2C–E.

claim: The impact of OCT4 loss on chromatin accessibility is consistent across the cell cycle.
source: Overall, these data show that the impact of OCT4 loss on chromatin accessibility is consistent across the cell cycle.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from the ATAC-seq data across different cell cycle phases.

claim: Residence times of OCT4 on specific DNA sites are in the second-range.
source: Since residence times of OCT4 on specific DNA sites are in the second-range (Chen et al., 2014; Teves et al., 2016; Deluz et al., 2016)
evidence: The manuscript cites Chen et al., 2014; Teves et al., 2016; Deluz et al., 2016 as support for this observation.

claim: At all OCT4-responsive clusters (1-3), accessibility loss was near-complete after 1 hr of IAA treatment.
source: At all OCT4-responsive clusters (1-3), accessibility loss was near-complete after 1 hr of IAA treatment (Figure 5A–B), in line with accessibility being highly dynamic with OCT4 levels.
evidence: The manuscript presents ATAC-seq time-course data shown in Figure 5A–B.

claim: At 6 and 10 hr of IAA treatment, cluster 4 sites that were insensitive to OCT4 degradation at the M-G1 transition started to lose accessibility.
source: At 6 and 10 hr of treatment, cluster 4 sites that were insensitive to OCT4 degradation at the M-G1 transition started to lose accessibility, suggesting a broader and potentially indirect impact of OCT4 loss on chromatin accessibility (Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript presents ATAC-seq time-course data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: At clusters 1–3, the half-life of accessibility loss was remarkably close to the half-life of OCT4-AID upon IAA treatment, that is around 0.5 hr.
source: At clusters 1–3, the half-life of accessibility loss was remarkably close to the half-life of OCT4-AID upon IAA treatment, that is around 0.5 hr (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: The manuscript presents exponential curve fitting analysis shown in Figure 5C–E.

claim: Both subnucleosomal reads (0–100 bp) and reads from single nucleosomes (180–250 bp) displayed reduced accessibility after 2 hr of IAA treatment.
source: Both categories of reads displayed reduced accessibility after 2 hr of IAA treatment, in line with these being bona fide changes in accessibility (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: The manuscript presents ATAC-seq fragment size analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–E.

claim: All genes close to loci in clusters 1 and 2, and two out of five genes close to loci in cluster 3, showed a small decrease in pre-mRNA levels after OCT4 depletion.
source: All genes close to loci in clusters 1 and 2, and two out of five genes close to loci in cluster 3, showed a small decrease in pre-mRNA levels after OCT4 depletion, although only one gene (Myc) showed a statistically significant (p<0.05) change (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Pre-mRNA levels of genes close to cluster 4 loci and mRNA (exon-exon) levels were generally unaffected by OCT4 depletion.
source: In contrast, pre-mRNA levels of genes close to cluster 4 loci and mRNA (exon-exon) levels were generally unaffected, and one control gene (Cntln) displayed a significant increase in mRNA levels after OCT4 depletion (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F–G and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F–G and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Rapid OCT4 depletion can impact transcription levels, particularly at genes close to loci regulated in accessibility by OCT4.
source: This indicates that rapid OCT4 depletion can impact transcription levels, particularly at genes close to loci regulated in accessibility by OCT4.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RT-qPCR data.

claim: Regulation of enhancer accessibility and activity is extremely dynamic and requires the constant presence of OCT4.
source: In summary, these data suggest that regulation of enhancer accessibility and activity is extremely dynamic and requires the constant presence of OCT4.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from the time-course experiments.

claim: A large number of enhancers are bound by both OCT4 and SOX2 but for which chromatin accessibility is regulated by only one of them.
source: In this study, we dissected the roles and interplay of OCT4 and SOX2 in regulating chromatin accessibility in ES cells. To our surprise, we found a large number of enhancers that were bound by both transcription factors but for which chromatin accessibility was regulated by only one of them.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the Results section.

claim: A larger influence on chromatin accessibility was found upon depletion of OCT4 than SOX2.
source: While we found a larger influence on chromatin accessibility upon depletion of OCT4 than SOX2, we cannot fully exclude that this is partly caused by differences in protein half-lives or cell lines.
evidence: This is a summary of findings with acknowledgment of potential confounding factors.

claim: Regions bound but not regulated by SOX2, including OD loci, could be controlled by other SOX family members such as SOX3 or SOX15.
source: Regions bound but not regulated by SOX2, including OD loci, could in principle also be controlled by other SOX family members such as SOX3 or SOX15 (Corsinotti et al., 2017; Masui et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation citing Corsinotti et al., 2017; Masui et al., 2007.

claim: Both OCT4 and SOX2 regulate the genomic occupancy of each other mainly via regulation of chromatin accessibility.
source: Our results also show that both OCT4 and SOX2 regulate the genomic occupancy of each other mainly via regulation of chromatin accessibility.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: This mechanism is reminiscent of dynamic assisted loading, in which two TFs assist the loading of each other to either the same or nearby DNA binding sites.
source: This is reminiscent of dynamic assisted loading, in which two TFs assist the loading of each other to either the same or nearby DNA binding sites (Swinstead et al., 2016; Goldstein et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites Swinstead et al., 2016; Goldstein et al., 2017 as support for this mechanism.

claim: Upon OCT4 loss, chromatin accessibility increased at a large number of genomic sites enriched for proximity to differentiation genes.
source: Surprisingly, upon OCT4 loss chromatin accessibility increased at a large number of genomic sites enriched for proximity to differentiation genes, even when OCT4 was degraded for only a brief period of time at the M-G1 transition.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the Results section.

claim: In the absence of OCT4, SOX2 is rerouted to differentiation-associated loci and promotes differentiation together with other partners such as TFAP2C.
source: The fact that SOX2 occupies these sites and is required to maintain their accessibility suggests that in the absence of OCT4, SOX2 is rerouted to these loci and promotes differentiation together with other partners such as TFAP2C.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The rapid action of OCT4 in early G1 phase might be required to ensure both the maintenance of chromatin accessibility at pluripotency enhancers and to silence differentiation enhancers.
source: Therefore, the rapid action of OCT4 in early G1 phase might be required to ensure both the maintenance of chromatin accessibility at pluripotency enhancers and to silence differentiation enhancers.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: OCT4 degradation led to a rapid decrease in chromatin accessibility at all clusters of OCT4-regulated enhancers across the cell cycle with very similar kinetics, which tightly mirrored changes in OCT4 concentration.
source: We found that OCT4 degradation led to a rapid decrease in chromatin accessibility at all clusters of OCT4-regulated enhancers across the cell cycle with very similar kinetics, which tightly mirrored changes in OCT4 concentration and thus suggests highly dynamic regulation of chromatin accessibility by OCT4.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the time-course experiments.

claim: The recovery of chromatin accessibility upon increase of OCT4 concentration displayed locus-dependent behavior.
source: However, the recovery of chromatin accessibility upon increase of OCT4 concentration displayed locus-dependent behavior.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the washout experiments.

claim: Loss across the whole cell cycle (cluster 3) or incomplete recovery (cluster 1) of chromatin accessibility may explain why OCT4 loss at the M-G1 transition results in impaired pluripotency maintenance.
source: While the mechanisms underlying these findings are unclear, loss across the whole cell cycle (cluster 3) or incomplete recovery (cluster 1) of chromatin accessibility may explain why OCT4 loss at the M-G1 transition results in impaired pluripotency maintenance.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The pioneering function of OCT4 is required constantly and throughout the cell cycle to maintain enhancer accessibility.
source: Here we expressed OCT4 at relatively low levels to ensure sufficient depletion, allowing us to show that the pioneering function of OCT4 is required constantly and throughout the cell cycle to maintain enhancer accessibility.
evidence: This is a summary of the main conclusion from the auxin-inducible degradation experiments.

claim: OCT4 is constantly required to maintain chromatin accessibility in self-renewing ES cells.
source: Here we found that OCT4 is constantly required to maintain chromatin accessibility in self-renewing ES cells.
evidence: This is a summary of the main conclusion from the study.

claim: The pioneer factor Zelda is required throughout zygotic genome activation in Drosophila for proper gene expression.
source: This is reminiscent of a recent study showing that the pioneer factor Zelda is required throughout zygotic genome activation in Drosophila for proper gene expression (McDaniel et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites McDaniel et al., 2019 as support for this observation.

claim: In the context of pituitary lineage specification, PAX7 requires 72 hr to fully open melanotrope-specific enhancers but is subsequently not required to maintain these.
source: In contrast, in the context of pituitary lineage specification PAX7 requires 72 hr to fully open melanotrope-specific enhancers but is subsequently not required to maintain these (Mayran et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites Mayran et al., 2018 as support for this observation.

claim: PAX7 may hand over the role of maintaining accessibility to other factors, such as TPIT.
source: It is possible that PAX7 hands over the role of maintaining accessibility to other factors, such as TPIT (Mayran et al., 2019), and is only required at the transition between cell fates.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation citing Mayran et al., 2019.

claim: Pioneering activity can have different manifestations that depend heavily on other regulatory factors and chromatin features.
source: This indicates that pioneering activity can have different manifestations that depend heavily on other regulatory factors and chromatin features.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing different systems.

claim: Pluripotent stem cells may be particularly dynamic in terms of chromatin accessibility regulation, as they need to be able to quickly rewire their gene expression programs upon receiving differentiation signals.
source: Pluripotent stem cells may be particularly dynamic in this regard, as they need to be able to quickly rewire their gene expression programs upon receiving differentiation signals.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the biological context.

claim: More differentiated cell types may have mechanisms to avoid precocious changes in gene expression upon subtle alterations in the concentration of TFs.
source: In contrast, more differentiated cell types may have mechanisms to avoid precocious changes in gene expression upon subtle alterations in the concentration of TFs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the biological context.

claim: The high sensitivity of enhancers to the concentration or activity of pioneer TFs in ES cells could serve as a mechanism to regulate cell fate with precise temporal control.
source: Therefore, the high sensitivity of enhancers to the concentration or activity of pioneer TFs in ES cells could serve as a mechanism to regulate cell fate with precise temporal control.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.
